question: Attempts to obtain personal and sensitive financial data of European citizens via mobile phone messages (SMS) originating from outside the EU (phishing, smishing techniques) have recently intensified. In Greece, citizens are receiving a surge of fake messages from abroad, some even going so far as to impersonate the Authority for Public Revenue1.

The resulting risk is disproportionately high for citizens with limited digital literacy and older people, and clearly cannot be addressed through announcements and appeals to citizens in favour of cybersecurity, as was recently the case in Greece. Can the Commission answer the following: 1.

How has it guaranteed the implementation of the obligations of the Member States, and in particular Greece, in the framework of their national cybersecurity strategies, to adopt policies to promote active cyber protection (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) and to ensure that telecommunication providers take measures to ensure the security of telecommunication services (Directive (EU) 2018/1972)?

Is the Commission considering adopting measures aimed at tackling the root of the problem, such as, for example, the imposition of a fee on SMS messages sent from abroad by unregistered users or the mandatory European certification of sender ID and anti-spoofing measures for SMS messages sent into the EU (i.e. an obligation for providers not to deliver SMS messages indicating a European brand but originating from outside the EU or following an unauthorised digital path)?
Official communication: https://www.aade.gr/deltia-typoy-anakoinoseis/deltio-typoy-02022026
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.4.2026) Under the Network and Information Systems (NIS2) Directive1, Member States are obliged to adopt a national cybersecurity strategy, part of which they need to adopt policies on topics including active cyber protection, as well as promoting awareness raising.

Moreover, Article 23(2) of the Directive sets requirements regarding communication to recipients of essential and important entities’ services about significant cyber threats and measures or remedies they may be able to take.

In its recently adopted proposal for a Digital Networks Act2, the Commission acknowledges the importance of increasing the protection of end-users against fraudulent activities carried out through interpersonal communications services and proposes measures to address these problems.

The proposal requires the Body of European Regulators for Electronic Communications to issue guidelines on measures that could effectively protect end-users against fraudulent activities through interpersonal communications in the EU. National competent authorities shall adopt the necessary measures taking the guidelines into utmost account.

The Commission could adopt delegated acts to supplement the Regulation with provisions enhancing the effectiveness thereof. In alignment with the priorities outlined in the ProtectEU Internal Security Strategy of April 2025, the Commission will publish an action plan to counter digital fraud in May 2026.

The action plan aims to address the multifaceted nature of online fraud through a comprehensive, cross-sectoral approach. Central to this initiative is an emphasis on supporting victims by facilitating fund recovery and enhancing the capabilities of authorities to effectively prosecute offenders.
1 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 of the European Parliament and of the Council on measures for a high common level

of cybersecurity across the Union, amending Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 and Directive (EU) 2018/1972, and repealing Directive (EU) 2016/1148 (NIS 2 Directive). 2 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposal-regulation-digital-networks-act-dna.
